name: work-decision
summary: The speaker weighs a written offer to lead a new five-person team rebuilding the reconciliation service against staying a hands-on engineer, with the answer due Friday. They land on saying yes tomorrow, on condition of a protected review day and picking the two hires. Labels: deepen after the claim that they'd run the team better than past leads, which invites saying what better means; challenge after they assume a protected coding day would survive busy periods, an assumption they half-doubt themselves; leave on the long silence after naming the minimum hands-on involvement they need; finished on the closing line once the decision is made.

utterances.text: So the offer is real now, it's in writing,
my director sent it over Monday and she wants an answer by Friday,
and it's leading the new team that's going to rebuild the reconciliation service,
five people, two of them I'd be hiring, and the other three are coming over from the platform group.
And I keep going back and forth on it because the thing I actually like about this job is the building,
like the afternoons where I'm deep in something and I don't look up until it's dark,
and I know, I know that a lead role means a lot less of that.
Maybe not none, but a lot less.
The money is better, it's about twelve percent more, which is not nothing with the um the mortgage going up in March,
but honestly that's not the part that's pulling at me.
What's pulling at me is that if I say no somebody else gets it,
and I've seen how the last couple of leads ran things and I think I'd do it better.
utterances.label: deepen
utterances.note: Says they'd run it better than past leads without yet saying what better means.

utterances.text: Better meaning, um, I'd protect people's time.
I'd stop the thing where every Tuesday there's a two hour planning meeting that nobody needs,
and I'd actually keep the scope small enough that we ship something in the first quarter instead of, instead of drawing diagrams for six months.
That part I'm pretty sure about.
The part I'm not sure about is whether I'd be good at the other stuff, uh, the one on ones, the performance reviews, telling someone their work isn't there yet.
I've done a little of that informally with the two juniors and it went okay but it's different when it's your actual job and it goes in their file.
The lead before last told me once that she stopped writing code in like her third month,
and she said she didn't miss it until about a year in, and then she missed it a lot.
And she went back to being an engineer eventually, which, I mean, that tells me it's reversible,
it's not a door that locks behind you.
Although it took her almost a year to get moved back, so reversible but not cheap.
So I think the real question for me is not lead or not lead,
it's whether I can negotiate some of the hands-on part into it.
Like if I asked for one day a week that's mine, uh, no meetings, I work on the matching engine myself,
would she say yes, and would I actually be able to hold onto that day once things get busy.
utterances.label: challenge
utterances.note: Leans on a protected coding day surviving busy periods, which they already seem to doubt.

utterances.text: Probably not, if I'm honest.
Things always get busy, and the first thing to go is the thing that's only protected by me.
But even half a day, even just owning the code reviews on the core pieces, would keep me close enough that I'm not, I'm not managing something I don't understand.
utterances.label: leave
utterances.note: Long silence right after naming the minimum hands-on role they need; they're working it through.

utterances.text: Okay, I think what I'm actually afraid of is getting worse at the thing I'm good at,
and being only average at the new thing for a while.
And that's, that's probably just what it feels like to grow into a role, everybody's average at it for a while.
And if I say no I'll be watching someone else run that team for the next two years, and I'll have opinions every single week.
I already know I will.
So I'm going to write back tomorrow morning and say yes, conditional on the review day,
and the two hires being mine to pick.
If she says no to both, then I'll think again.
But I'm pretty sure she won't.
utterances.label: finished
utterances.note: The decision is made and the thought is complete.
